abstract: This lecture covers infant gastroesophageal reflux (GER) versus gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), emphasizing that most infants are 'happy spitters' whose symptoms peak at 3 months and resolve by 1 year. Dr. Keller reviews red flags requiring further evaluation (bilious vomiting, forceful vomiting, blood, poor weight gain, aspiration), conservative management (smaller frequent feedings, upright positioning, nipple flow adjustments, thickened feeds with oat cereal), and formula selection including hypoallergenic options for cow's milk protein allergy. The talk also addresses differential diagnoses such as pyloric stenosis, Sandifer syndrome, and mimics of blood in the diaper (urate crystals), as well as two related allergic conditions: IgE-mediated cow's milk protein allergy and non-IgE-mediated food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome.
key_points: About 80% of infants are 'happy spitters'; physiologic reflux peaks at 3 months and resolves by 1 year of age.
Bilious vomiting indicates small bowel obstruction until proven otherwise, requiring immediate evaluation.
Poor weight gain is the most common presentation of GERD in the clinic; feeding logs help assess caloric adequacy and food insecurity.
Thicken feeds with dry infant oat cereal (not rice cereal) at 1 tablespoon per ounce; do not use thickeners in breast milk because amylase digests them.
Positional therapy is limited: upright 20-30 minutes after feeds helps, but crib wedges and head propping are not recommended due to SIDS risk.
40% of infants with GERD have cow's milk protein allergy; trial of hypoallergenic formula (extensively hydrolyzed or amino acid-based) is indicated when reflux is excessive.
Watch for Sandifer syndrome: arching, neck extension, and chin lifting during or after feeds, signaling esophageal pain from reflux.
Urate crystals in the diaper (gritty, brick-red, not shiny) mimic blood in the first 1-3 days of life and are normal.
Bright red blood per rectum ± streaks in stool may indicate anal fissure, proctocolitis, or cow's milk protein allergy; perform a spread-sheet exam.
Food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES) is non-IgE mediated, presents with vomiting and diarrhea hours after milk/soy/rice/oats, and is distinct from typical IgE-mediated allergy.
Most infants are 'happy spitters' who do not lose weight and require only parental reassurance.
Conservative measures (e.g., upright positioning, avoiding overfeeding) and a trial of hypoallergenic formula (or maternal dairy elimination if breastfeeding) should precede pharmacotherapy.
